title: The north falls (2 Kings 17)
hookLine: Assyria takes Samaria and the northern tribes are carried away and scattered

cards: One chapter, and a kingdom ends. All week this path has been in the north, Israel, with its capital at Samaria. Elisha asked for pi shnayim, and his teacher's cloak fell to him.
A woman in Shunem built a little room on her roof for a holy man. A proud general washed in the Jordan because a captive girl spoke up. A frightened servant had his eyes opened.
Four lepers carried good news to a starving city. Today, in one chapter, that kingdom ends.

teach.b: The last king of the north is named Hoshea. He stops paying tribute to Assyria and looks to Egypt for help. The king of Assyria marches in, besieges Samaria and takes it.

He carries the people of Israel away into Assyria, and settles them in distant places the text names: Halah, and Habor by the river of Gozan, and the cities of the Medes. Then the chapter does something unusual.
It stops telling the story and starts explaining it.
The writer's answer is long and blunt: the people had turned to other gods, though the Lord had warned Israel and Judah by every prophet and every seer: turn from your evil ways. They would not hear.

teach.h: NONE LEFT BUT THE TRIBE OF JUDAH.
teach.b: And then one sad line: "there was none left but the tribe of Judah only." The king of Assyria brings people from other lands to live in the empty towns of Samaria. The map is redrawn.
Those carried away never come back in the story; the book of Kings simply goes on with Judah. Later readers would call them the lost tribes, and tradition tells stories about where they went.
But the prophets didn't let the north be forgotten.

teach.h: TWO STICKS JOINED IN ONE HAND.
teach.b: Ezekiel is told to take two sticks, one for Judah and one for Joseph, and join them into one in his hand. Jewish tradition keeps that hope alive: one day, the scattered come home. The lost tribes are lost to the record.
They were not lost to memory.

how: Jews read 2 Kings 17 as part of the Former Prophets, and the hope that the scattered tribes will one day be gathered appears in the prophets and in Jewish prayer.

s: the text says where the northern tribes were settled
it names Halah, Habor by the river of Gozan, and the cities of the Medes.
the book of Kings follows the northern exiles to their new homes
it goes silent about them and carries on with Judah.
the chapter stops the story to explain why the north fell

games.q: you're the writer of Kings. the northern kingdom has just fallen. what do you write next?
o: stop the story and explain why it happened.
follow the exiles to their new lands.
games.why: the chapter pauses the story for a long explanation: the people turned away, though every prophet and seer had warned them.

practice: Bring to mind people whose names nobody wrote down: great-great-grandparents you can't name, a town that isn't on the map anymore, the workers who built a place you walk past every day.

You don't need faces or details; with each slow breath, let one of them be real for a moment, people who cooked, worried, laughed, and were carried off by time. If you pray, you can remember them before God.

wordCard.voice: Hoshea, the last king of the northern kingdom, whose revolt against Assyria brought the siege that carried Israel away and ended the north.

orig.note: Hebrew: exile, the word Jewish tradition uses for life scattered away from the land.

carryVoice: Your line: the lost tribes. The north is gone from the story, not from the hope. Good to see you today.
